newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy 97 CPI seen unlikely below 2.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy 97 CPI seen unlikely below 2.6 pct.

text.p: Italian consumer price inflation will improve further in 1997 with the average annual rate falling to 2.6 percent from 3.9 percent in 1996 in line with the Bank of Italy's goal of a rate below 3.0 percent, analysts said.
The government's official target is for an average 2.5 percent for 1997. But it is difficult to foresee a fall below 2.6 percent, a Reuter quarterly poll of 18 analysts showed.

In fact, analysts expect on average to see a 2.8 percent CPI rate for 1998, higher than current levels and expectations for 1997. Inflation in December was steady on November at 2.6 percent year-on-year.
In the previous Reuter quarterly poll, analysts had on average forecast 1997 inflation at 2.9 percent.

An eventual dip below 2.6/2.5 percent this year "will also depend on inflation rates abroad," said Paolo Casadio of Credito Italiano. "There is a barrier not only for Italy at 2.5 percent, but also for the whole of Europe at around 2.0 percent."

According to Marco Ratti of Banca Commerciale Italiana, "Growth is slow at the start of 1997 but the situation will improve progressively in the second half with a resulting rise in inflation to support foreign demand and domestic investment demand. Domestic consumer demand will add to this in 1998."

For 1997, the cost of labour - a variable many analysts believe the Bank of Italy is currently watching closely with regard to a move on key interest rates - is seen as a negative factor for the economy, though having little effect on CPI.

The second quarter of 1997 should see CPI at its lowest level of the year but in the second half of the year prices should start rising gradually, "but this will not be a sudden, alarming hike," said Lucia Trevisan of Caboto brokers.
"For 1997 I see strong deflationary pressure. I am negative about global growth and on the general economic trend," said Gianluca Sanna of Banco di Sardegna.

"I see average annual consumer prices rising 2.5 percent. Favouring this are the strong exchange rate and moderate consumer demand while on the negative side there will be an acceleration in labour costs," said Ilaria Fornari of J.P. Morgan.
Casadio saw consumer prices this year reflecting fundamentals more closely after some abnormalities in 1995 and 1996.

He saw producer prices having more of an effect on inflation, with PPI growing 1.9 percent due to labour costs and companies restoring profit margins. But raw materials and oil prices were expected to be under control and the exchange rate would remain strong.
However, an increase of below two percent in PPI would be "compatible with CPI at 2.6 percent," Casadio added.
